outcomes: Names the enemy pieces that can use what a pawn move gives up
Judges an unlabeled pawn move as harmless or costly, including moves that give up nothing important
Explains why the same kind of move is fine in one position and bad in another
sources: items IBds54-2..7 (engine depth 16, pawn_attackers and attackers claims after the move), IP-SQ-102 (structure claims)

steps.text: This lesson builds on **What a pawn move leaves behind**. There you marked the squares a pawn move stops guarding. Now add the second question: **who can use them?** A move that leaves a square unguarded is costly only if an enemy piece attacks it or can get there. If none can, the move may be harmless.

steps.title: Two pawn moves, one position
steps.prompt: White thinks of g3 in the first position and of g4 in the second; the position is the same. Predict, then check.

steps.text: Ask three things. What does the pawn stop guarding? Which enemy pieces attack those squares, or can reach them? Does the move gain something concrete, such as driving off an attacker? **Rule of thumb:** a pawn move is costly when an enemy piece can use the squares at once. Near your own king, no pawn move is automatically safe.
Now without hints. Some pawn moves cost nothing and some cost a lot. Look at the squares the pawn guarded, then at the enemy pieces. A harmless move gives you a plain *yes*.

steps.prompt: Before you answered the silent items, what did you look at first: the pawn's squares, or the enemy pieces? Write one pawn move that you rejected too fast, or accepted too fast, and why.
